🎬 Two video creation modes: Model Engine vs Code Engine

One stickman director, two ways to create your visuals: A uses video models to generate continuous shots; B uses code to animate layered assets. With the right tools, an AI agent can take either approach through to a finished video, following the selected style’s specifications.

A · Model Engine B · Code Engine
Concept Feeds prompts and storyboards into video generation models to render fluid video clips directly. Generates layered visual assets, then writes and executes code to animate, compose, and render locally.
Features Fluid natural motion and cinematic lighting; vivid visuals with rich cinematic dynamics. Stable character consistency with reusable assets; precise timeline pacing, layout control, and easy local fine-tuning.
Best for Creators with access to video generation resources (e.g., Google Flow, affordable APIs, or self-hosted local models), focusing on visually striking short-form content. Users with active Codex or Claude Code subscriptions looking to put surplus coding quota to work—without paying extra for expensive video model credits.
Workflow Confirm script and style to get scene prompts for manual generation; or let your agent operate a built-in browser to generate clips, stitch scenes, and handle captions & audio. Confirm the video script and a 20s sample for the chosen style, then let your agent automatically handle all asset preparation, code authoring, animation execution, captions, audio, and local rendering.
Output Storyboard script + scene prompts + (full video file) Layered asset library (characters/scenes/props) + full video file
Cost Consumes video model generation credits/points; longer videos scale significantly in cost and re-roll overhead. Zero video model credits needed; renders locally using your existing agent quota and basic image/TTS tools.

Start with an idea, an article, a web link, or a complete script. Both modes support short videos and longer content. Choose 16:9 landscape or 9:16 portrait for your publishing platform, and configure captions, voiceover, background music, and sound effects to suit your needs and the selected style.

Still deciding on a style? Below, you’ll find detailed descriptions, suggested topics, and more sample videos for each style.

Generate assets, edit, and polish your video right in the conversation—no editing software required—and get a finished video ready to publish. Visit Renoise to explore its models and creative tools.

🧭 Get started

For results as close as possible to the sample videos, we recommend AI tools with strong coding capabilities, such as Codex or Claude Code.

You can also use this skill with other agents that can read and write files and run commands. Results may vary with the model’s capabilities, tool setup, and execution approach.

Step 1: Install the skill

On first use, your agent will check the required setup and help you install or configure anything missing. Send the following to your AI agent:

Help me install this skill:
https://github.com/kaomei/stickman-video-director

After installation, read SKILL.md and tell me you’re ready.

If you prefer the terminal or the installation times out, you can refer to the manual installation guide.

Step 2: Choose a style and mode, then start with a prompt

Choose a style you like from Model Engine (A) or Code Engine (B), then copy the corresponding prompt below, adapt it to your needs, and send it to your AI agent:

A · Model Engine

Use Model Engine (A) to turn the following topic or text into a stickman video:
[Enter a topic, paste your text, or describe your idea]

Requirements: 16:9 landscape, style A3 “Prehistoric Cave.” Start with a 30-second video.

First, give me a story outline, an audio plan, and a storyboard.
After I approve them, provide self-contained video generation prompts for each scene.
  • Production workflow: After approving the storyboard, you can generate the clips manually or ask your agent to generate them using its browser tools. Start with a low-resolution test. Once you approve the result, your agent can handle the remaining clips and assemble the full video, adding captions and audio as needed.
  • Recommended platform: Use Google Flow to get closer to the sample results. For your first video, see the detailed tutorial on X.

B · Code Engine

Use Code Engine (B) to turn the following topic or article into an engaging stickman video:
[Paste an article, a news story, or a link, or describe your topic]

Requirements: 16:9 landscape, 8 minutes, style B1 “Minimal Line Art,” with voiceover, captions, and sound effects.

First, check that the local tools for image generation and rendering are set up. Then provide a complete script and a preview of the opening 20 seconds with audio.
After I approve both, automatically prepare all assets, write the code, and render the complete video locally.
  • Production workflow: After you approve the script and the preview of the opening 20 seconds with audio, the agent prepares the assets, animation, captions, and audio to match the selected style, then renders the full video locally and provides a preview.
  • Targeted edits: If you’re unhappy with part of the visuals or audio, ask your agent to adjust just that section while keeping the approved parts.

Step 3: Create a thumbnail, title, and description

Once you’re happy with the finished video, continue with the Thumbnail & Publishing Kit. Send this to your agent:

Create a thumbnail, video title, description, and pinned comment for the video we just made, using the approved visual style.

The AI will generate a matching thumbnail, video title, description, and pinned comment in one step, without switching modes or reconfiguring your setup.

🎨 A · Model Engine Overview

The current Model Engine (A) samples were created with Google Flow. You can also choose another video generation platform. Before asking your agent to produce a video automatically, make sure you’re logged in and have available credits.

Styles are numbered A1, A2, A3… Each style includes its own animated samples.

A1: Classic Black & White

A round head and a handful of lines can make a complicated idea click. With the clutter stripped away, every gesture and visual metaphor matters: anxiety becomes a cage; attention becomes a battery running low.

  • The look: Crisp black ink on white, or a more dramatic white-on-black version. A few bright accents put the important detail in focus.
  • Made for: Science, psychology, personal growth, business breakdowns, and concepts that become clearer with the right visual analogy.
A1.1 · Black on white A1.2 · White on black
Pure white canvas · Black characters Pure black canvas · White characters

A2: Modern Pop

Red beanie. Yellow shirt. A character you recognize at a glance. Follow them from floating tech interfaces into city streets and the wilderness, turning a tool demo or a personal turning point into a character-led story.

  • The look: Minimal Tech pairs white space with glass-like interfaces and cyan light. Colorful Story adds richer settings, depth, and mood-driven lighting.
  • Made for: AI tools, tech products, tutorials, personal growth, everyday experiences, and adventures.
A2.1 · Minimal Tech A2.2 · Colorful Story
White space · Faint grid · Cyan glow Colorful scenes · Cinematic lighting · Story atmosphere

A3: Prehistoric Cave

No phones. No offices. So why are the cavemen still stuck working? Visually inspired by YouTube’s @Zenn0009 (200K subscribers). Drop modern problems into a world of caves, campfires, and animal skins, and watch familiar frustrations turn into absurd little stories with a sting.

  • The look: Rough hand-drawn lines, earthy settings, and big reactions. Character interactions, reaction shots, and comic pauses do the storytelling.
  • Made for: Workplace satire, human nature, prehistoric what-ifs, dark comedy, fables, and English-learning stories for children.
Example 1: "How Did Humans Get Their First Job?" Example 2: "The First Discovery of Fire"
Prehistoric story · Workplace twist Discovery of fire · Community creation

A4: Cozy Storytelling

The message you feel you must answer. The afternoon you finally keep for yourself. Small moments in stations, bedrooms, and corner cafés give hard-to-name feelings a place to live—and viewers a chance to recognize themselves.

  • The look: Colorful everyday settings, gentle light, and understated gestures. A close-up catches hesitation; a wider shot leaves room to breathe.
  • Made for: Relationships, everyday emotions, personal growth, habits, and warm stories that still make room for anxiety and exhaustion.
Example 1: Message anxiety on the commute Example 2: Making time for yourself
Subway station · Walking shots · Emotional close-ups Outdoor café · Warm light · Everyday gestures

A5: Historical Cartoon

Samurai have bills to pay. An Egyptian cat can steal the scene. Step into the streets, temples, and camps of the past, turning a historical detail into something a character actually has to deal with.

  • The look: White round heads, bold ink outlines, and colorful period settings. Costumes, buildings, and props establish the era; reactions and playful contrasts bring it to life.
  • Made for: World history, curious civilizations, everyday life in the past, historical figures, and humorous history shorts.
Example 1: Edo Japan · A samurai's everyday life Example 2: Ancient Egypt · Cats and mummies
Edo streets · Samurai clothing · Everyday contrasts Colorful temples · Black cat characters · History with a twist

Style and prompt contribution: Lawal Ridwan / @leksautomate.

A6: Amber Noir

What if you woke up and everything cost ten thousand times less? The visual inspiration is YouTube's @IfverseTales (60K subscribers gained in 3 weeks). An orange-hooded figure moves through golden light and deep plum shadows, turning a casual hypothetical into a cinematic story about temptation, consequences, and unexpected turns.

  • The look: Amber highlights, dark silhouettes, and layered city scenes. Character actions and restrained camera movement build curiosity without a talking presenter.
  • Made for: What-if scenarios, modern fables, psychology, unexpected discoveries, and stories with a twist.
Example 1: What if everything cost 10,000 times less? Example 2: The Era of Collapsing Prices
Renoise MCP example · 20 seconds · Narrated by Tim Google Flow example · 8 seconds · Model-native audio

A7: Rubber Hose Animation

A fine-line stickman steps into richly drawn vintage scenery, turning everyday mishaps into theatrical comedy through elastic gestures, expressive faces and continuous character acting. Muted sage, ivory and tiny faded-red accents preserve the period charm while keeping the actor clear.

  • The look: A consistent white circular face, two curved hair tufts and a thin-line body; confident ink contours, matte painted textures, prop interaction and expressive editing.
  • Made for: Absurd comedy, everyday fables, twist stories and music-led shorts.
Example 1: Chased by a cloud Example 2: A rainy street
Vintage hand-drawn streets · Elastic character acting Rainy atmosphere · Prop interaction and reaction cuts

A8: Studio Ghibli Style

Deep blue skies and seas, towering clouds, and sun-warmed stone walls set the scene for these hand-painted adventures. A sea breeze ripples the laundry and lifts the awnings. When a letter flies out of a messenger’s satchel, an ordinary ride turns into a little adventure.

  • The look: Textured gouache backgrounds, rich blocks of color, and crisp shadows frame stick figures drawn in the flat colors of traditional cel animation. Round heads, dot eyes, and thin ink-line limbs keep the figures simple.
  • Made for: Travel stories, everyday adventures, stories about working life, and fables with a touch of whimsy.
Demo 1: Mountain Workshop Demo 2: Seaside Messenger
Wide mountain views · Wind and rope work Painted coastal streets · Cycling and catching a letter

A9: Coming soon…

New Model Engine styles are in preparation. Star the project to follow future updates.

🤖 B · Code Engine Overview

All current Code Engine (B) samples were made with Codex: its built-in image model, gpt-image-2, generates the visual assets, then code drives the layered animation and renders the video locally. Before asking another agent to produce a video automatically, make sure it can read and write files, execute terminal commands, and has the required tools configured.

Styles are numbered B1, B2, B3… Each style includes its own complete sample videos. Names such as Bodi, Fola, Brian, Claire and The Pharaoh 3 in the sample captions are the text-to-speech voices used for those samples; you can choose any voice.

B1: Minimal Line Art

Like a friend sketching an idea as they explain it. Expressive faces, black linework, and a few colorful props turn abstract knowledge into little scenes—and product benefits into situations people recognize.

  • The look: Near-white paper, lively hand-drawn marks, and purposeful headline text. Expressions, props, and subtle animation carry the explanation without crowding the screen.
  • Made for: YouTube explainers, education, psychology, personal growth, workplace stories, and product introductions.
Example 1: YouTube without showing your face Example 2: Posting Every Day—Why Is Nobody Watching?
Hand-drawn characters · Key text · Subtle animation Google Gemini · Bodi voiceover · Expressive faces · Subtle animation

B2: Colorful Hand-Drawn

Why does your mind get louder the harder you try to sleep? Inspired by YouTube's @PsychToonsHQ (200K subscribers), warm paper textures, soft colors, and handwritten touches turn sleeplessness, procrastination, and distraction into little stories that feel uncomfortably familiar.

  • The look: Fine ink lines, colorful everyday settings, and ivory paper captions. Close-ups, illustrated metaphors, and gentle motion reveal the psychology behind a small habit.
  • Made for: Everyday psychology, sleep, habits, attention, personal growth, and relatable life explainers.
Example 1: Why Does Trying to Sleep Keep You Awake? Example 2: You Unlocked Your Phone—and Forgot Why
Bedtime thoughts · Scenic cutaways · Gentle motion Google Gemini · Everyday distractions · Colorful scenes · Fola narration

B3: Retro TV

Like stumbling across a curious late-night broadcast. Inspired by YouTube's @BradikininVideos (55K subscribers gained in 3 weeks), rounded white-and-gray characters, faint bloom, and analog texture turn an ordinary question into a satisfying discovery.

  • The look: Luminous figures against dark screens, clean white text, and subtle scanlines. Scene changes and small reactions give science a playful edge—and strange events a little suspense.
  • Made for: Everyday science, psychology, animal behavior, curious facts, and short mysteries.
Example 1: What if your TV turns on at 3 AM? Example 2: Is Your Dog Guilty—or Just Scared?
Fictional suspense · Scene changes · TV texture Google Gemini · Animal behavior · Local reactions · Bodi narration

B4: Survival Thriller

A countdown. A late-night call. A rule you must never break. Ordinary places become traps in a look inspired by YouTube's @BeanieSurvives (100K subscribers gained in 3 weeks). Round white heads, white gloves, and stark light and shadow give simple characters an unsettling world to inhabit.

  • The look: Half-shadowed openings, unnerving close-ups, and threats emerging from the dark. Small changes in expression, light, and props build suspense without explaining every image.
  • The sound: The narrator (the Brian voice) draws you in from the opening. A quiet, continuous ambient bed carries the tension; story-driven effects make the danger audible without overwhelming the narration.
  • Made for: Survival rules, urban legends, disaster escapes, and suspense with a twist.
Example 1: 911 Dispatcher Rules: Do Not Send Police Example 2: What if you saw death coming?
Brian narration · Story-synced SFX · A cliffhanger choice A chilling visual hook · Impactful text animation

B5: Avatar Explainer

Give your favorite avatar a starring role. (Using a well-known character requires permission.) Your presenter takes the mic in the corner while expressive stickmen act out the idea—dragged around by bills, flattened by pressure, or caught in a visual punchline. Even abstract ideas become something viewers can see and remember.

  • The look: Warm paper textures, a distinctive presenter, and bold black-and-red type. Exaggerated weight, recoil, and transforming props turn explanations into visual metaphors.
  • The sound: Clear narration leads, with lip sync, expressions, and captions following the voice. Sound effects land on the action; light music stays out of the way.
